title: API Rate Limiter
brief: Design a rate limiter for a public API: protect the backend from abuse and stampedes while staying invisible to well-behaved users. The interviewer cares about correctness under distribution and what happens when things fail.
requirements: Per-user limits (e.g. 100 requests/min), enforced across the whole fleet
Well-behaved users must not notice it (sub-millisecond overhead)
Over-limit requests get a clear 429 response

rounds.question: One clarifying question before you design. Which answer changes the architecture most?

options.conceptLabel: Is the limit per-user across ALL servers, or per single server?
options.rationale: This is the fork in the road: per-server limits need only local memory, but a fleet-wide per-user limit forces shared state — which drags in a store, atomicity, and a failure story. Everything downstream depends on this answer.

options.conceptLabel: Which HTTP status code should rejected requests get?
options.rationale: It's 429 by convention — a one-line detail with zero architectural consequence. Burning your clarifying question on it tells the interviewer you can't rank concerns.

options.conceptLabel: Which web framework do the API servers use?
options.rationale: The limiter should sit in front of (or beside) the app regardless of framework. Framework choice changes an import statement, not the design.

options.conceptLabel: How many endpoints does the API expose?
options.rationale: Endpoint count barely matters — limits key on the caller, not the route (per-route limits are a config detail on the same machinery). It doesn't reshape any component.

rounds.question: Where in the request path does the limiter belong?

options.conceptLabel: In the gateway/middleware layer, checked BEFORE the request does any real work
options.rationale: The whole point is to shed abusive load cheaply. A gateway check rejects in microseconds, before the request touches app logic or the database — one enforcement point, uniform across every endpoint.

options.conceptLabel: Inside each endpoint handler, per route
options.rationale: N endpoints means N chances to forget one, and the request has already paid routing, auth, and app-server capacity before being rejected. Enforcement belongs at the boundary, once.

options.conceptLabel: In the client SDK, before the request is sent
options.rationale: Client-side limiting is a courtesy, not a control — anyone with curl bypasses it entirely. The abusers you're designing against are exactly the ones who won't run your SDK.

options.conceptLabel: In the database layer, rolling back over-limit queries
options.rationale: By the time the database sees the query, the request has consumed everything you were trying to protect. Rejecting after the work is done is load-shedding theater.

rounds.question: Which algorithm tracks each user's usage with O(1) memory and smooth limiting?

options.conceptLabel: Token bucket — a refill rate plus a burst allowance, two numbers per user
options.rationale: Tokens refill at the steady rate and the bucket depth permits honest bursts; state is just (tokens, last-refill-time). Sliding-window counters are the other fine answer — the key property is O(1) state with no boundary spikes.

options.conceptLabel: Fixed window counter — reset the count every minute on the clock
options.rationale: The classic boundary bug: 100 requests at 11:59:59 plus 100 more at 12:00:01 is 200 requests in two seconds, all allowed. Simple, but it permits exactly the burst you were hired to stop.

options.conceptLabel: Sliding window log — store the timestamp of every request
options.rationale: Perfectly accurate and perfectly unbounded: memory grows with request rate (100 timestamps per user per minute, times millions of users). The accuracy isn't worth O(requests) state.

options.conceptLabel: Leaky bucket as an actual queue that delays requests
options.rationale: Queueing over-limit requests instead of rejecting them turns your rate limiter into a latency machine and the queue into an unbounded buffer during abuse — the exact stampede amplifier you're defending against.

rounds.question: Limits are fleet-wide, so counters must be shared. Where does that state live?

options.conceptLabel: A centralized in-memory store (Redis) with atomic ops, sharded by user
options.rationale: Atomic INCR/EXPIRE (or a small Lua script for token math) makes check-and-update race-free, sub-millisecond, and sharding by user key spreads the load. This is the industry-standard shape.

options.conceptLabel: Each gateway node's local memory
options.rationale: With N gateways behind a load balancer, a user's requests scatter across all of them — each node sees 1/N of the traffic and the real limit silently becomes N × 100/min. Local state can't enforce a global limit.

options.conceptLabel: The primary SQL database with row locks
options.rationale: 10k req/s of lock-update-commit on hot user rows will melt the database you built the limiter to protect. Durable storage and ACID are the wrong tools for ephemeral counters.

options.conceptLabel: A config file on each server, re-synced every minute
options.rationale: Counters change thousands of times per second; a minute-stale file is not state, it's a snapshot of history. File sync is for configuration, not for live coordination.

rounds.question: Redis goes down. Fail open (allow everything) or fail closed (reject everything)?

options.conceptLabel: Fail open with a fallback: allow traffic, alert loudly, degrade to coarse per-node limits
options.rationale: For most public APIs a few minutes of unenforced limits beats a self-inflicted total outage — the limiter is protection, not the product. Local per-node caps keep worst-case abuse bounded while Redis recovers.

options.conceptLabel: Fail closed — reject every request until Redis returns
options.rationale: You just turned a cache outage into a 100% API outage: the rate limiter DDoSed your own product. Fail-closed is for security gates (auth), not for load protection.

options.conceptLabel: Retry Redis synchronously until it answers
options.rationale: Blocking every request on a down dependency stacks up threads and timeouts until the gateways themselves fall over — you've converted a partial failure into a cascading one.

options.conceptLabel: Disable rate limiting permanently after the first failure
options.rationale: Failing open needs to be a temporary, alarmed, self-healing state. A one-way kill switch means one blip and your API runs unprotected forever — nobody will remember to turn it back on.
